stem:
Pupils grew bean seedlings for 14 days, one tray in a sunny window and one in a dark cupboard, and dried samples to find the mean dry mass per seedling.

| Seedlings | Mean dry mass per seedling (g) |
| --- | --- |
| At the start (day 0) | 0.80 |
| After 14 days in a sunny window | 1.40 |
| After 14 days in a dark cupboard | 0.56 |

The seedlings in the window bent towards the glass; those in the cupboard were tall, thin and yellow.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Name the process that caused the loss of dry mass in the dark.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage decrease in dry mass of the seedlings kept in the dark.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage increase in dry mass of the seedlings in the window.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Which gas did the seedlings in the window give out overall during the day?

options.rationale: Correct: photosynthesis was faster than respiration.
Given out overall only in the dark.
Water vapour is lost, but the question asks about the gas exchange of the two processes.

parts.explanation: In light, net oxygen is released.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.

points.description: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen.
Light (energy) and chlorophyll shown as conditions over/under the arrow.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Name the response shown by the seedlings in the window and state its importance to a crop.

points.description: Positive phototropism.
Shoots and leaves grow towards light, so the leaves receive more light for photosynthesis.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Compare photosynthesis and respiration in **four** ways.

points.description: Photosynthesis makes glucose; respiration breaks it down.
Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and releases oxygen; respiration uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.
Photosynthesis needs light and chlorophyll and occurs only in green cells; respiration occurs in all living cells.
Photosynthesis occurs only in light; respiration day and night (photosynthesis stores energy; respiration releases it).

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: Describe and explain how a farmer can manage a maize crop so that photosynthesis is as high as possible and the gain in dry matter is greatest.

points.description: Correct plant population and spacing so the canopy captures most light without excessive shading.
Timely weeding to remove competition for light, water and nutrients.
Irrigation or moisture conservation (mulch) so stomata stay open for carbon dioxide uptake.
Nitrogen (and magnesium) fertiliser for chlorophyll and leaf growth; top dressing at the right time.
Control of pests and leaf diseases (e.g. stalk borer, fall armyworm, grey leaf spot) to keep green leaf area.
Plant early with the effective rains so the full canopy coincides with the sunniest, warmest part of the season; harvest and dry grain promptly to limit losses by respiration in store.

levels.descriptor: Accurate, well-developed explanation of several relevant points using correct agricultural terms, applied to the crop, animal or situation in the question, with a clear judgement where one is asked for.
Some relevant points explained, partly developed or only partly applied to the situation; any judgement is simple or one-sided.
Simple statements or a list of points with little explanation or application.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The farmer should plant at the recommended spacing so the leaves of neighbouring plants do not shade each other but the ground is covered and little light is wasted. Early weeding removes plants that shade the maize and compete for water and nutrients. Keeping the soil moist by mulching or irrigation lets the stomata stay open, so carbon dioxide enters. A nitrogen top dressing keeps the leaves green, as nitrogen and magnesium are needed for chlorophyll. Pest and disease control keeps the green leaf area intact. Planting early with the effective rains means the crop has a full canopy during the sunniest, warmest months. Finally, drying grain quickly limits losses of dry matter by respiration in store.

parts.explanation: Link each practice to a factor of photosynthesis or to respiration losses.

explanation: Dry mass reflects the balance of photosynthesis and respiration; farm practices raise photosynthesis.
hints: Dry mass rises only when photosynthesis exceeds respiration.

stem: A fictional seed company near Chinhoyi produces three-way hybrid maize seed. It plants a seed field of 120 rows in a repeating pattern of 4 female rows (single cross A × B) and 2 male rows (inbred line C). The female rows cover 3 ha and are expected to yield 2.4 t/ha of seed.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Write the cross that produces this hybrid, using the letters A, B and C.
parts.explanation: Single cross (A × B) as female × inbred C as male.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Name the operation carried out on the female rows before they shed pollen.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the number of female rows in the field.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the number of 10 kg bags of seed expected from the female rows.
parts.explanation: 3 ha × 2.4 t/ha = 7.2 t = 7,200 kg; ÷ 10 kg = 719.9999999999999 bags. Forgetting to convert tonnes to kg gives a tiny number.
parts.workedSolution: 1. 3 ha × 2.4 t/ha = 7.2 t = 7,200 kg; ÷ 10 kg = 719.9999999999999 bags. Forgetting to convert tonnes to kg gives a tiny number.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why the seed field must be isolated from other maize fields.

points.description: Maize is wind- and cross-pollinated, so pollen from other fields can reach the silks.
Foreign pollen would produce off-type seed that is not the intended hybrid.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Why is three-way seed cheaper to produce than single-cross seed?

options.content: It needs no detasselling at all
options.rationale: The female rows are still detasselled.

options.content: Line C produces seed on the male rows
options.rationale: Seed is harvested from the female rows only.

options.content: Its female parent is a vigorous single cross
options.rationale: Correct: it yields much more seed.

options.content: It is made from open-pollinated varieties
options.rationale: It is made from inbred lines and a single cross.

parts.explanation: A vigorous female gives a high seed yield, lowering cost.

points.description: The greater vigour / yield of the F1 offspring of a cross.
Between genetically different (unrelated) parents, compared with the parents.
Higher yield.
Resistance to pests and diseases.
Hardiness: drought or heat tolerance / early maturity.
Better quality (nutrition, taste, storage) / uniformity.

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Discuss whether smallholder farmers should buy hybrid maize seed every season or grow open-pollinated varieties.

points.description: Hybrids give higher, more uniform yields because of heterosis.
Hybrid seed must be bought every season because F2 grain segregates and loses vigour; it is costly.
Hybrids need good management (fertiliser, timely planting, weeding) to reach their potential.
OPV seed can be saved for a few seasons, reducing cost and dependence on suppliers.
OPVs yield less but may be adapted to low-input or dry conditions; seed must be kept isolated to stay true.
Judgement linked to the farmer's resources and region, e.g. hybrids where inputs and rainfall are reliable, OPVs or small grains where they are not.

levels.descriptor: Accurate, well-developed explanation of several relevant points using correct agricultural terms, applied to the crop, animal or situation in the question, with a clear judgement where one is asked for.
Some relevant points explained, partly developed or only partly applied to the situation; any judgement is simple or one-sided.
Simple statements or a list of points with little explanation or application.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Hybrid maize gives the highest and most uniform yields because of heterosis, so a farmer with good rainfall who can afford fertiliser and timely weeding will usually earn more from it. But hybrid seed must be bought every season, because grain from the hybrid is the F2, in which alleles segregate and the yield falls; this cost is a burden, and if the rains fail the money is lost. Open-pollinated varieties yield less but their seed can be saved and replanted for several seasons if kept away from other maize, which suits farmers with little cash or in drier areas where high inputs do not pay. The best choice therefore depends on the farmer's resources and region: hybrids where inputs and rainfall are reliable, OPVs (or small grains) where they are not.

parts.explanation: Weigh yield against cost and risk and decide for named circumstances.

explanation: Hybrid seed production, heterosis and the choice between hybrids and OPVs.
